strengths: The UniEM-3M dataset is a genuinely useful resource for the materials-vision community: 5,091 EM images with ~3M instance-level segmentation labels and 9-dimension structured text, which is far larger and denser than prior EM datasets (Table 1) such as EMPS (465 images) or Aversa et al. (22k images with only class labels).

The dataset construction pipeline is well documented, including perceptual-hash deduplication, resolution/quality filtering, GPT-based removal of embedded metadata text, a semi-automated Gemini/GPT attribute-extraction and cross-check protocol (Figs. 9-10), and a human-in-the-loop annotation workflow with peer review and expert audit.

The paper provides useful statistical characterization of the dataset (Figs. 2, 3, 11, 12), including long-tail coverage of materials, morphologies, particle densities, image resolutions, and instance-area distributions, which supports the claim of scale and heterogeneity.

The generative component is evaluated from multiple angles (FID, DINOv2 style similarity, t-SNE overlap in Fig. 7, and a downstream pretraining experiment in Fig. 6 / Table 3) and the Gen+Real combination yields a measurable improvement (0.807/0.705), which is a reasonable, if limited, demonstration that the synthetic data is usable.

UniEM-Net (flow-based, Cellpose-style 2D vector fields with SAM-ViT backbone) is competitive on both sparse and dense subsets (0.824/0.720 and 0.787/0.703, Table 2), and the qualitative results in Figs. 4, 5, 13 convincingly show that anchor-based and prior field-based methods degrade on dense, low-contrast, and irregular morphologies.
weaknesses: The dataset release is only partial ('a subset of UniEM-3M will be made publicly available'), which is a serious limitation for a dataset/benchmark contribution. The community cannot reproduce the reported benchmarks, verify the annotation statistics, or extend the work without the full annotations and images. The proposed diffusion model is positioned as a 'proxy for the complete data distribution' and a 'privacy-preserving surrogate,' but this framing is scientifically dubious for EM micrographs and does not substitute for actual data access.

The novelty of UniEM-Net is limited: it is explicitly an adaptation of Cellpose ('Inspired by Cellpose') with a SAM-ViT backbone, and the described training/inference pipeline (energy function, x/y gradients, Euler integration, probability map) is largely inherited from that line of work. The claimed algorithmic contribution is therefore incremental relative to the dataset.

The baseline comparison in Table 2 is not fully controlled. UniEM-Net (93M params) is compared against Cellpose-SAM (304M) and other methods with very different backbones and training regimes, so the reported 'outperforms other advanced methods' claim conflates architectural differences with method differences. There is no ablation isolating the flow-based component, and no comparison to recent segmentation foundation models (e.g., SAM with prompts, SAM 2, DINOv2-based or domain-specific EM segmenters).

Annotation quality is not rigorously quantified. The pipeline relies heavily on model-generated pseudo-labels refined by annotators, yet the paper reports no inter-annotator agreement, no human-vs-model label agreement, and no breakdown of how many of the ~3M instances were fully human-verified versus model-proposed. This is a critical omission for a dataset paper, especially since downstream benchmark numbers on partially pseudo-labeled ground truth can be optimistically biased.

The text descriptions are produced by Gemini/GPT with cross-checking, but their scientific correctness is not evaluated quantitatively. There is no measurement of attribute accuracy (e.g., against expert labels on a held-out sample), which weakens the claims about 'structured, decoupled, high-fidelity' annotations and about their value for vision-language modeling.

The generative-model claims are overreaching relative to the evidence. The 'novel out-of-distribution samples' produced by attribute recombination (Fig. 8b) are not validated by materials experts or by any physically meaningful criterion, and the FID/style-similarity metrics are computed only against the model's own training distribution, not against any external reference. The privacy motivation for EM images is unsubstantiated.

Several claims of 'universality' are overstated relative to the reported statistics: Fig. 11(a) shows ~90.9% of images are SEM, with only ~3.7% TEM and ~2.9% other modalities, and the dataset is a mix of web-crawled and literature-sourced images, raising concerns about licensing and about representativeness of acquisition conditions.

There is no cross-dataset generalization experiment (training on UniEM-3M and testing on EMPS, MMSci, or other EM sets), which is one of the most informative evaluations for a dataset paper and would substantiate the claim that models trained on this data transfer broadly.

Some presentation issues reduce clarity: key figures (Figs. 11, 12) have very small fonts; the 'SA1B-pretrained' baseline is used in Fig. 6 without definition; and the related work section is brief and omits substantial prior work on EM/SEM segmentation, synthetic EM data generation, and materials vision-language datasets.

strengths: Introduces UniEM-3M, a large-scale EM dataset with 5,091 high-resolution images and ~3M instance segmentation annotations, addressing a genuine scarcity of instance-level annotated microscopy data for materials science.

The data engine is thorough: multi-source collection, perceptual-hash deduplication, quality filtering, embedded-text removal, structured LLM-assisted attribute extraction with expert cross-checking, and a custom high-density annotation platform with human-in-the-loop quality control.

Comprehensive benchmark of representative instance segmentation methods, including anchor-based, anchor-free, and 2D field-based approaches, with sparse/dense splits; UniEM-Net achieves strong mAP/PQ while using fewer parameters than Cellpose-SAM.

The SDXL-LoRA generative model is well motivated and evaluated with FID, style similarity, t-SNE, and downstream segmentation gains, providing a useful augmentation and surrogate tool for sensitive EM data.
The paper is clearly written and accompanied by extensive supplementary details on prompts, annotation, statistics, and implementation, which supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset is only partially released: the abstract states that 'a subset of which will be made publicly available' and describes a 'partial dataset,' which limits benchmark reproducibility and weakens the dataset contribution. Licensing, copyright, and consent details for web-crawled and collaborative images are not discussed.

Potential test-set leakage: the generative model is described as trained on 'the entire collection,' and generated data are then used to train segmentation models while evaluation is on test images from the same collection. Unless the generative model is restricted to the training split, reported gains may be inflated.

The instance segmentation metric is nonstandard: AP is defined as TP/(TP+FP+FN) per image and averaged, which is not standard mask AP over confidence-ranked detections; PQ is also borrowed from panoptic segmentation without full justification. This makes reported mAP/PQ values and SOTA claims difficult to compare with prior work.

Annotation quality is not quantitatively validated: no inter-annotator agreement, text-description accuracy, or label-error analysis is reported, despite heavy reliance on LLM-generated descriptions and pseudo-labels.

Dense-scene comparison is incomplete: anchor-based methods are excluded from the dense subset due to NMS/computational limits, so the claim that flow-based methods are superior in dense microscopy is only partially supported.

The train/test split appears random and no cross-material or cross-source evaluation is provided, so the dataset's claimed universality and generalization to unseen material systems are not fully tested.
The privacy-preserving surrogate claim is not validated; no membership inference or leakage analysis is provided, and the generative model may still memorize or reveal sensitive training data.
The algorithmic novelty of UniEM-Net is limited: it is largely based on Cellpose/SAM with directional-field flow, and architecture/training details are sparse relative to the dataset contribution.
No limitations or societal-impact discussion is included, and the paper does not address potential biases in LLM-generated attribute labels or long-tailed material coverage.

strengths: Substantial data-construction effort: 5,091 high-resolution EMs with roughly 3 million instance annotations addresses a genuine scarcity of instance-level EM data for materials science, and the focus on extreme instance density (thousands of objects per image) targets a real failure mode of existing methods.

The benchmark is reasonably broad, covering anchor-based, anchor-free, and 2D-field segmentation methods, with a useful sparse/dense split that exposes how NMS- and proposal-based detectors break down in crowded scenes (Table 2, Fig. 4-5).

The human-in-the-loop annotation pipeline and bespoke web-based tooling (Sections 8, 12) are a practical contribution for high-density microstructure annotation, and the structured attribute schema (Fig. 9-10) is a sensible foundation for materials-oriented vision-language modeling.
The paper is generally well organized and the statistical analyses of instance count/area distributions (Figs. 2-3, 11-12) help characterize the dataset's difficulty and long-tailed composition.
weaknesses: The core deliverable is not actually released: the abstract and contributions state that only 'a subset' of UniEM-3M will be made publicly available, with a diffusion model offered as a 'proxy for the complete data distribution.' For a dataset/benchmark paper this is a fundamental problem: the Table 2 benchmark and all segmentation experiments use the full collection, so independent verification and fair use of the benchmark are impossible. The 'large-scale' claim is also weakened because the public subset size is never specified.

UniEM-Net has limited novelty: Section 3.1 describes essentially an adaptation of CellPose-style flow/energy fields (x-y gradients, Euler integration, probability map) with a SAM-ViT backbone. No architectural innovation is claimed, and no ablation isolates the contribution of the energy/field formulation versus the backbone or training data, so it is unclear whether the gains are methodological.

The comparison in Table 2 is not backbone- or budget-controlled (UniEM-Net 93M vs CellPose-SAM 304M vs CellViT 146M), and UniEM-Net is trained/evaluated on the full dataset while others are 'fine-tuned' for only 72 epochs. The claim that 'flow-based models outperform' is therefore not cleanly established, and the paper itself concedes comparisons 'are not fully controlled.'

Validation of the generative model is weak. FID is computed with an ImageNet-trained Inception network on grayscale micrographs, which is methodologically questionable for this domain; the 'style' cosine-similarity metric is a weak proxy. The downstream benefit is marginal (0.800 -> 0.807 mAP when adding 30K generated images, Table 3), so the strong claims about augmentation/proxy value are not well supported.

Textual annotations are produced by LLM prompting (Gemini/GPT) with model-vs-model 'cross-checking' and expert resolution of discrepancies, but no quantitative validation is given (no inter-annotator agreement, no accuracy against a human gold standard). The reliability of these 'attribute-disentangled' descriptions, which are central to the multimodal claim, is therefore unverified.

Key experimental gaps: no cross-dataset generalization (e.g., training on UniEM-3M and testing on other EM datasets), no comparison against recent EM-specific segmentation approaches beyond those listed, and no evaluation of the generative model or text descriptions by domain experts.

The 'privacy-preserving surrogate' framing is misapplied: materials micrographs do not raise the personal-privacy concerns the introduction invokes, and the paper does not address licensing/copyright or consent for web-crawled and industrially sourced images, which is a real concern for a dataset release.

The 'first large-scale and multimodal' EM dataset claim is contestable given MMSci (~100K images with text). The paper's distinction rests on raw, instance-level labels, but the framing overstates the novelty, and annotation quality is never quantified despite relying heavily on model-assisted pseudo-labels.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, high-quality, and multimodal electron microscopy dataset (EM3M) with ~3 million instance segmentation annotations, addressing a significant data scarcity problem in materials science computer vision.

The multimodal integration of image-level textual descriptions with disentangled attributes (using LLMs and human verification) provides a valuable structured foundation for future vision-language modeling in this domain.

The dataset curation and annotation pipeline is rigorous, employing a human-in-the-loop strategy with detailed inter-annotator agreement metrics and quality control stages to ensure annotation fidelity.

Demonstrates the practical utility of a text-to-image diffusion model (via SDXL LoRA fine-tuning) as a data augmentation engine, showing that synthetic data can effectively supplement real data to improve downstream segmentation performance.

Establishes a strong and well-motivated baseline (UniAIMS) that appropriately addresses the specific challenges of the dataset (extreme instance density and scale variation) by modifying the Cellpose framework and removing its size model.

Provides a comprehensive benchmark of representative instance segmentation paradigms (detection-based, query-based, bottom-up), revealing the limitations of current state-of-the-art models on dense microstructural scenes.
weaknesses: While the paper proposes a strong baseline (UniAIMS), the architectural changes are primarily engineering adaptations to Cellpose (such as removing the scale model and adopting multi-GPU training/backbone upgrades) rather than fundamentally new algorithmic contributions.

The reliance on proprietary LLMs (Gemini and GPT) for the initial semi-automated generation of structured text descriptions may pose minor reproducibility challenges for the exact text annotation pipeline, despite providing the prompt templates.

Although the paper addresses it in the 'Open Problems' section, the severe performance drop at higher IoU thresholds (e.g., PQ@90 dropping to 0.340) indicates that precise boundary delineation for dense, fine-grained microstructures remains largely unsolved, which limits immediate practical applicability for certain high-precision metrology tasks.

strengths: The paper introduces EM3M, a large-scale electron microscopy dataset with 5,091 images and approximately 3 million instance-level segmentation annotations, significantly advancing data availability for microstructural analysis.

It provides multimodal image-text data with structured attribute descriptions and a semi-automated annotation pipeline supported by human-in-the-loop quality control, including inter-annotator agreement statistics and expert validation.

The work presents a thorough benchmark across detection-based, query-based, and bottom-up segmentation paradigms, revealing that flow-based bottom-up methods are better suited to dense, highly instance-rich EM scenes.

It contributes a text-to-image diffusion augmentation engine for EM data and demonstrates that synthetic data improves downstream segmentation and pretraining performance, supported by FID, style-similarity, t-SNE, and ablation studies.
The proposed UniAIMS baseline is well motivated for the dataset's scale variation and density challenges, with practical adaptations and strong empirical results.

The manuscript is clear, includes comprehensive dataset statistics, open problems, implementation details, and reproducibility-oriented descriptions, making the contribution accessible and useful to the community.
weaknesses: Benchmark fairness is limited: detection-based and query-based methods are evaluated only on a sparse subset (<100 instances), while bottom-up methods are evaluated on the full dataset, so the reported comparison is not entirely apples-to-apples.

The generative augmentation is validated mainly through FID, style similarity, and t-SNE overlap; these metrics do not fully establish physical validity or absence of hallucinated microstructures, which matters for materials science applications.

Text attribute annotations are produced using Gemini/GPT with human review, but only a 300-image subset is independently re-annotated; large-scale annotation reliability and possible LLM hallucinations remain uncertain.
UniAIMS is largely an engineering adaptation of Cellpose with modified scale handling, backbone, and training infrastructure; the algorithmic novelty relative to its base framework is modest.

Dataset release and licensing details are not fully specified in the provided manuscript, and some images derive from academic/industrial collaborations or web crawling, raising potential reproducibility and redistribution concerns.

Evaluation metrics use a non-COCO AP definition and report PQ mainly at 0.5 IoU; the paper itself notes a large drop under stricter PQ@90, indicating that benchmark saturation and fine-grained quality assessment are not fully resolved.

strengths: The paper introduces a substantial and potentially useful resource: 5,091 electron micrographs with approximately 3M instance segmentation annotations and structured image-level text, addressing a real scarcity in materials-oriented microscopy.

It documents a multi-stage data engine, human-in-the-loop annotation, inter-annotator agreement, statistical analyses of material/morphology/density, and a benchmark of representative instance segmentation methods.
The generative augmentation component is interesting, and the public release of the dataset, baseline, and generative model is valuable for reproducibility.
The UniAIMS baseline and cross-dataset evaluation provide a practical starting point for future work.
weaknesses: Benchmark fairness is limited: detection- and query-based methods are evaluated only on a sparse subset (<100 instances) while bottom-up methods and UniAIMS are evaluated on the full dataset, so the headline comparison does not directly establish superiority under the dense scenes that motivate the paper. This is a major concern for the benchmark contribution.

UniAIMS is largely an engineering adaptation of Cellpose (removing the size model, adding LSJ augmentation, multi-GPU training, ViT-Base backbone), and it is compared against Cellpose trained under different resource constraints, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed method rather than confounding factors.

Text modality is one of three claimed contributions, yet the LLM-generated structured attributes lack quantitative quality or consistency evaluation beyond human review and cross-checking; no downstream vision-language task is used to validate them, so the multimodal claim is under-supported.

The dataset split is random at image level, without grouping by sample, source, or acquisition session; this risks train/test leakage and inflated benchmark performance, especially for images sourced from multiple views of the same specimen.
Licensing, attribution, and ethics of web-crawled data and re-annotated public data are not sufficiently discussed, which is problematic for a public dataset release.
Generated-data gains are modest (e.g., Gen+Real 0.809 mAP vs. Real 0.800 mAP) and are not supported by statistical significance or error bars, making the augmentation claim weaker than presented.
